sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Chain-of-thought reasoning has revolutionized natural language processing by enabling large language models (LLMs) to decompose problems into intermediate steps before answering. Yet confining reasoning to the textual domain presents limitations for tasks requiring direct manipulation of visual representations. Recent efforts augment multimodal LLMs with external visual expert tools such as depth estimation or object detection modules, but these remain fundamentally limited by their reliance on narrow, rigid operations that cannot flexibly generate or transform visual content. We propose ReImaGin, which leverages image generation models as a flexible visual reasoning mechanism for multimodal LLMs: unlike fixed-function tools, they accept natural language commands and can perform open-ended visual operations, like removing an occlusion or generating a floorplan from multiple disjoint views of a room. Across six diverse visual reasoning tasks including multi-view spatial reasoning and collision prediction, ReImaGin consistently outperforms both text-only reasoning and specialist vision-tool baselines, with gains of up to 25\%, demonstrating the advantage of flexible, generative visual reasoning.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Chain-of-Thought (CoT; Wei et al. (2022)) reasoning has emerged as paradigm shift in natural language processing, significantly enhancing the capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) by enabling them to generate intermediate reasoning rationales. This success has naturally extended to the multimodal domain, driving impressive performance gains in tasks such as Visual Question Answering (VQA) (Zhang et al., 2023; Lu et al., 2022; Alayrac et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2023; Dai et al., 2023). However, the vast majority of existing multimodal frameworks restrict the reasoning process to the textual domain, essentially describing visual inputs in words and processing them logically (Alayrac et al., 2022; Li et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023; Dai et al., 2023). While effective for some tasks, this text-centric approach is ill-suited for tasks that demand spatial or physical intuition, such as visualizing the removal of occlusions or novel view synthesis. To overcome the limitations of purely textual reasoning, recent works have begun augmenting Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) with external visual tools, such as modules for cropping, depth estimation, and object detection (Hu et al., 2024; Fu et al., 2025). These frameworks allow model to execute basic visual operations to support its reasoning process. However, this approach suffers from two limitations. The primary limitation is the rigidity of the tools provided: these frameworks rely on pre-defined modules that can identify bounding box or segment an object, but are unable to perform flexible, generative, or complex transformations (e.g., imagining an alternative view of scene). Consequently, the reasoning process remains limited by the static and narrow nature of the underlying toolset. second limitation is that models are typically taught to use these tools via handcrafted in-context examples, adding manual effort and limiting generalization to new tasks. To address the narrow capabilities of traditional visual tools, we explore new framework: reasoning with image generation. Unlike fixed-function tools that are limited to predetermined set of operations (e.g., segmentation, depth estimation), recent generative models are trained to follow instructions in natural language, enabling them to perform vast and open-ended range of visual operations that can be expressed linguistically (Deepmind, 2025; Black Forest Labs, 2025; Wu et al., 2025). This flexibility is transformative: single generative model integrates the capabilities of many specialist vision tools (e.g., segmentation and depth estimation) while also producing arbitrary visualizations and image transformations that were previously out of reach, such as alternative views or blueprint of room, without any task-specific specialization. Crucially, the capabilities of this approach scale directly with advances in visual generation: as generative models become more capable, the range of ways the agent can reason visually expands accordingly. We instantiate this idea as REIMAGIN, multimodal agent that interleaves textual chain-ofthought with calls to an instruction-tuned image generation model. The agent is equipped with free-form generate_image tool that can be invoked at any reasoning step with natural language prompt, returning visual intermediate directly into the agents context (see Figure 1). For instance, on collision prediction task, the agent might call generate_image to draw trajectory line from the moving object, then inspect the resulting image to identify which object the line first intersects (Figure 4). Unlike specialist vision tools, which expose fixed set of operations, the same generate_image tool can perform broad range of visual transformations, based on the natural-language prompt it receives. Beyond the core framework, we also investigate question that the flexibility of generative tools raises. Because generate_image accepts arbitrary natural-language instructions, the agent can perform vast range of transformations; the question is which transformation actually helps for given task. As noted earlier, standard practice is to specify the transformation through handcrafted in-context examples that demonstrate the desired strategy (e.g., generate depth map for depth reasoning). This requires manual effort per task and limits generalization to new tasks. As complementary exploration, we ask whether such strategies can be discovered automatically. Since the strategy is conveyed to the agent through its prompt, discovering strategy reduces to optimizing the prompt: we instantiate an iterative loop in which proposal model generates candidate prompts, evaluates them on small development set, and refines based on observed successes and failures. Published as conference paper at COLM 2026 We evaluate REIMAGIN on six diverse visual reasoning tasks spanning depth perception (Fu et al., 2024), visual puzzle completion (Zhou et al., 2025), counting under partial occlusion (Pothiraj et al., 2025), collision prediction (Wang et al., 2025c), multi-view spatial reasoning (Yang et al., 2025), and path tracing task that we introduce. The same image generation model serves as the tool across all tasks, performing transformations ranging from depth map generation to occlusion removal and floorplan synthesis, without any taskspecific specialization. Across tasks and MLLMs, REIMAGIN with handcrafted strategies consistently improves over both text-only reasoning and reasoning with fixed visual tools, specifically Visual Sketchpad (Hu et al., 2024), by up to 25% on path tracing and 40% relative on counting under partial occlusion. Further, automatically discovered strategies often resemble those human would design (e.g., drawing an arrow from the front of moving object to predict collisions), suggesting that MLLMs have useful priors about which visual transformations aid given task. These discovered strategies recover most of the gains of handcrafted ones without any human-crafted examples, though gap remains on tasks that benefit from more elaborate visual reasoning policies. Our contributions are three-fold: 1. We propose REIMAGIN, multimodal agent framework that equips an MLLM with free-form image generation tool. Unlike prior work that relies on fixed specialist modules, the generative tool supports far wider and more flexible range of visual transformations. 2. Using this same generalist tool across six diverse visual reasoning tasks, we show that REIMAGIN consistently improves over text-only reasoning and reasoning with expert image tools (i.e. Visual Sketchpad). 3. We additionally show that effective visual reasoning strategies can be discovered automatically via prompt optimization, recovering most of the gains of handcrafted strategies and often resembling them, which suggests MLLMs have useful priors about which visual transformations aid given task.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Prior work equips multimodal LLMs with fixed specialist vision tools such as crop, detection, segmentation, or depth estimation (Hu et al., 2024; Fu et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025b; Zheng et al., 2025), but each tool performs narrow, pre-specified transformation, so the agent can only apply manipulations implemented in advance. separate line of work iteratively refines generated images (Yang et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025; Khan et al., 2025; Wan et al., 2025), where the image is the final object being optimized rather than an intermediate for downstream question. Closest to us, recent methods reason with generative or latent visual models (Li et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2026; He et al., 2025; Gu et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026; Qin et al., 2025), but they typically require task-specific training, target single narrow domain, or reason in non-interpretable latent space. In contrast, REIMAGIN is training-free and modular: it invokes single instruction-following image generator for open-ended transformations, carries out its visual reasoning in interpretable pixel space, and is evaluated across six diverse visual reasoning tasks. We provide an extended discussion in Appendix A.

sections.title: 3 REIMAGIN - Reasoning with Image Generation
sections.content: We present REIMAGIN, multimodal agent framework that uses instruction-following generative models to produce visualizations within an iterative reasoning loop. The agent can use the generative model by calling the generate_image function, in addition to standard programmatic image tools (e.g., crop, overlay, subtract, and libraries like numpy), within python environment. Unlike prior tool-augmented approaches, such as Visual Sketchpad (Hu et al., 2024), which depend on fixed suite of specialist vision models (e.g., depth estimator, segmenter, object detector) each confined to its own narrow task, REIMAGIN leverages an instruction-following generative model that can flexibly perform wide range of operations through natural language. sections.title: 3.1 Agent Architecture
sections.content: Our agent architecture builds upon the ReAct framework (Yao et al., 2022), illustrated in Figure 6 (Appendix C). We describe each component below, and provide an example in Appendix E. Prompt. At each turn, an MLLM receives prompt consisting of three components: tool descriptions that define the available tools, in-context examples that illustrate how to apply visual reasoning to solve the task, and the context Ct comprising the query, input images, and prior turn history. Reasoning step. At each turn the MLLM receives Ct and produces chain-of-thought rationale θt that interprets the previous context and reasons about the next action. Action step. Based on θt, the agent emits Python program αt that is executed at runtime. The program may call programmatic image utilities (e.g., crop, overlay), the generative tool generate_image, and general-purpose code (e.g., numpy for pixel-level analysis). We retain the cheap, deterministic programmatic utilities alongside the generative tool for simple transformations; some tasks compose both, e.g., the puzzle task (Figure 2) uses generate_image to remove whitespace and subtract_images to isolate the missing piece. Image generation tool. The generate_image tool accepts text prompt and, optionally, one or more reference images, which are passed to an instruction-following image generation model that returns new synthesized image. Context update and termination. The outputs of αt (including any generated images) are appended to the agents context as new user message before the next turn. The loop continues until the agent appends TERMINATE to its rationale θt, at which point the final answer is parsed from the preceding text. Improving Image Generation via Test-Time Scaling. Image generation is stochastic, and variance grows with task difficulty: simple edits such as occlusion removal are consistent across samples, whereas harder transformations such as floorplan creation can yield very different layouts. Since reasoning accuracy depends on the faithfulness of the generated image, we exploit this stochasticity as test-time scaling: generate_image samples candi4 Published as conference paper at COLM 2026 dates independently and uses an MLLM to select the one that most faithfully satisfies the prompt (Karthik et al., 2023). From the agents perspective the interface is unchangedit always receives single image back. Figure 7 (Appendix F) illustrates this. Whereas prior test-time scaling draws multiple text chain-of-thought traces and aggregates them via majority voting or best-of-N (Brown et al., 2024; Singhi et al., 2025; Snell et al., 2024), we instead sample single reasoning trace and spend the extra compute on improving the generated images. Multiple CoTs could be sampled for additional test-time compute.

sections.title: 3.2 Automated Discovery of Visual Reasoning Strategies
sections.content: An important element in our framework is deciding which visual transformations the agent uses to benefit reasoning. The potential of visual reasoning is maximized when good solution strategy is used. For example, in the path tracing task, dashed lines can confuse MLLMs. Realizing that, e.g., making the lines solid significantly simplifies the reasoning, can be very important. Prior work (Hu et al., 2024) relies exclusively on hand-crafted strategies for how and when to use the various individual tools in order to help answer the question. While effective, hand-crafted strategies require task-specific human effort and reintroduce human-in-the-loop bottleneck. To reduce this bottleneck, we ask whether effective visual reasoning strategies can instead be discovered automatically. Since the strategy is conveyed to the agent through its prompt (i.e., through tool definitions and in-context examples that demonstrate when and how to invoke each tool), discovering strategy reduces to finding prompt that induces effective tool use. We therefore formulate automated strategy discovery as an iterative search over agent prompts. Given task τ with training split Dtrain and development split Ddev, the goal is to obtain prompt that induces effective visual reasoning for fixed reasoning agent AR. The search is initialized from the baseline No Strategy prompt, which includes the standard tool definitions but no task-specific visual reasoning policy. At round r, the search maintains set of candidate prompts Pr. Each round alternates between two stages: candidate prompt evaluation and candidate prompt proposal. In the candidate prompt evaluation stage, we run AR with each prompt Pr on both Dtrain and Ddev. Ground-truth answers are used to compute the task metric and identify successful and failed trajectories. Examples of failure and successful attemps on the training are seen during the proposal stage to refine the strategies. The development score J(p) is used for selection of the top strategies. In the candidate prompt proposal stage, proposal agent AP receives the retained prompts together with selected successful and failed trajectories drawn from the training split Dtrain, and proposes new prompts intended to improve the tool use. The best prompt across rounds is returned as p. Throughout the search, AR and the image generator remain fixed; only the agent prompt is optimized. We use the same guidance for candidate prompt proposal for all tasks, as shown in Figure 16. Notably, the optimization receives no human-authored task-specific strategy or reasoning trace.

sections.title: 4 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Tasks. We evaluate on six tasks spanning visual reasoning problems that require spatial understanding and visual transformations. Depth Reasoning (BLINK; Fu et al. (2024)) tests relative depth perception: given an image with two marked points, the model must predict which point is closer to the camera. Puzzle Completion (MIRA; Zhou et al. (2025)) presents an image with missing region alongside five candidate pieces, and the model must identify which piece fits the gap perfectly. Occlusion Counting (CAPTURE; Pothiraj et al. (2025)) shows multiple instances of an object category, some occluded by black square, and the model must count them all, including the hidden ones. Collision Prediction (Spatial457; Wang et al. (2025c)) presents overhead-view scenes and asks which object target would collide with if it moved forward or backward. Spatial Reasoning (MMSI; (Yang et al., 2025)) presents two partially overlapping views of an indoor scene and asks about the relative positions of objects or regions across them; we use the Pos (Obj-Obj) and Pos (Obj-Reg) splits. Path Tracing is task we introduce: each image contains four numbers (14) and four 5 Published as conference paper at COLM 2026 letters (AD) at random locations, each number connected to one letter by dashed line, and the model must identify which letter each number connects to (Figure 4). Additional details about each task are provided in Appendix B. Models. As the MLLM backbone we use Gemini-3.1-Pro (The Gemini Team, 2026) and GPT-5 (OpenAI, 2025) as proprietary models, and Qwen-3.5-27B (Qwen Team, 2026) as an open-weights alternative. As the visual generative tool, our primary model is Nano-BananaPro (Gemini-3-Pro-Image; Deepmind (2025)), state-of-the-art instruction-tuned image generation model. We additionally experiment with two open-weights generative models: FLUX.2 [dev] (Black Forest Labs, 2025) and Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 (Wu et al., 2025). For image-generation test-time scaling, we use Gemini-3.1-Pro as the selector. Baselines. We compare against two baselines. No Tools is vanilla MLLM that answers directly from the input query and images, without access to any tools or code execution. Visual Sketchpad (Hu et al., 2024) augments the MLLM with fixed toolbox of specialist vision modules and programmatic manipulation tools, but does not include any open-ended generative visual capability. On the spatial task (MMSI), REIMAGIN applies test-time scaling to image generation (Section 3.1); to match this test-time budget, the two baselines receive comparable compute via majority vote over 20 sampled answers. Metrics. All tasks use multiple-choice accuracy, except Occlusion Counting, for which we report symmetric mean absolute percentage error (sMAPE) (Pothiraj et al., 2025) , sMAPE = 100(y ˆy)/(y + ˆy) , where and ˆy are the predicted and ground truth counts. We report metrics averaged over 3 seeds, along with the standard error across these runs. All prompts used in our experiments are provided in Appendix N. Automated Discovery of Visual Reasoning Strategies. Here, we compare Handcrafted Strategy, using the default human-designed visual reasoning policy, No Strategy (employs image generation without task-specific guidance), and our Automatic Strategy, using policy discovered from development feedback. We perform visual reasoning strategy discovery with at most Dtrain = 50 and Ddev = 50 samples, less on MMSI due to dataset size limitations. We run the search for = 4 rounds and create 5 candidate prompt proposals in each round. In practice, both the proposal agent AP and the reasoning agent AR are instantiated with the same model. In our experiments, we used Gemini-3.1-Pro or Qwen3.5-27B. The proposal context retains the top 2 prompts found so far, and each included prompt context block contributes 2 incorrect and 2 correct examples from Dtrain, as well as other success and failure examples from the last round. We implement the strategydiscovery loop using Opik (Comet ML, 2024). Full prompts and details on the one-time discovery cost of approximately $214 per task are deferred to Appendix L.

For spatial reasoning (MMSI), REIMAGIN first stitches the two input images into unified view, then generates top-down perspective of the scene to make spatial relationships explicit (Figure 2, top). This task poses particular challenge for the generative model: the required geometric operations are difficult, and the generated layouts vary significantly across samples (as shown in Figure 8, Appendix F). To address this, we leverage test-time scaling (as defined in Section 3.1) with = 10 samples, selecting the most faithful generation rather than relying on single output. Figure 3 illustrates the impact across models: without test-time scaling, REIMAGIN achieves 51.0% on Gemini-3.1-Pro and 42.0% on Qwen-3.5-27B. With test-time scaling, performance improves substantially to 59.0% and 54.3% respectively. Importantly, test-time scaling only affects the generated images and leaves the rest of the reasoning process unchanged, demonstrating that more faithful visualizations directly translate to better downstream performance. Even with the baselines given matched test-time compute (Section 4), REIMAGIN still outperforms both across all three MLLMs (e.g., 59.0% vs. 57.0% on Gemini-3.1-Pro and 54.3% vs. 46.7% on Qwen-3.5-27B). The other five tasks show little variance across generated samples (Figures 9 and 10, Appendix F): repeated calls produce consistent outputs, so the selector has nothing meaningful to choose between, and additional sampling cannot improve faithfulness. We accordingly do not apply test-time scaling on these tasks. Figure 3: Effect of test-time scaling on spatial reasoning across models. Sampling multiple candidate generations improves accuracy for all three MLLMs. Open-weights image generation models. We fix Gemini-3.1-Pro as the MLLM and swap in two open-weights alternatives, FLUX.2 [dev] (Black Forest Labs, 2025) and Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 (Wu et al., 2025), evaluating each across all tasks  (Table 2)  . These errors persist even when the generator succeeds, and scale with MLLM capability rather than with generation quality, as shown in Table 1.

sections.content: Reasoning with generated images requires strategy for deciding when visualization is needed, what visualization to generate, and how to use it afterward. We therefore explore whether such strategies can also be discovered automatically, following our approach presented in Section 3.2; results appear in Table 3. We evaluate discovery in two regimes. The first pairs the strong Gemini-3.1-Pro MLLM (The Gemini Team, 2026), used as both proposal model and task-solving agent, with the strong Nano-Banana-Pro generator (Deepmind, 2025). The second pairs the weaker open-weights Qwen-3.5-27B MLLM (Qwen Team, 2026), again used for both proposal and task solving, with the flash version of the image generator, Nano-Banana-2 (Gemini-3.1-Flash-Image; Google (2026)). With the stronger pairing, it also consistently outperforms the No Strategy setup, where the MLLM is given access to the generative image tool but no specific strategy. Together, these results show that the discovery procedure can produce useful task strategies across varying reasoning and image-generation model capabilities. As illustrated in Figure 5, discovered strategies often closely match the handcrafted ones. For instance, the optimized depth prompt learns to generate depth map, and the collision prompt learns to draw an arrow from the front of the object that will collide with another. These small differences in wording result in only small drops relative to the handcrafted baselines. In cases where the difference between the discovered and handcrafted strategies is larger, the gap widens: for path tracing, our handcrafted strategy simply makes dashed lines solid, whereas the optimized strategy additionally colors them. Because Nano-BananaPro rarely fails to make lines solid but more frequently fails to color them correctly, this richer strategy slightly degrades performance. Similarly, the composite strategy we use for 9 Published as conference paper at COLM 2026 Figure 5: Automatically discovered visual reasoning strategies. Discovered strategies are frequently similar to handcrafted ones (generate panorama, solid lines), with some differences (color the lines). Appendix contains more qualitative examples of success and failure cases of discovered strategies. MMSI spatial reasoning is not recovered under the current search setting, although useful strategy that requests panorama-like view of the room is discovered. The independently Qwen-discovered prompts exhibit the same qualitative pattern (Appendix L). Appendix provides the discovery meta prompt and the discovered strategies. Cross-MLLM transfer. We further test whether strategy discovery is tied to the MLLM used during optimization, or whether discovered strategy can in fact be used by different MLLM with different reasoning capabilities. To test this, we use the Gemini-3.1Pro-discovered prompts unchanged with Qwen-3.5-27B, without rediscovery, as shown in Table 4. The transferred strategies outperform No Tools on all five tasks, and Visual Sketchpad and No Strategy on collision, spatial reasoning (MMSI), and path tracing. Because the prompts are applied unchanged, these gains show that their utility generalizes beyond the MLLM used during discovery. However, as seen by the degraded performance on Occlusion counting and the lack of improvement in Depth, visual reasoning strategy optimized for an MLLM with strong perceptual and reasoning capabilities can sometimes fall short of bringing the same benefits when paired with weaker model.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced REIMAGIN, multimodal reasoning framework that uses image generation as flexible mechanism for visual reasoning. Rather than restricting reasoning to text or relying on fixed set of specialist visual tools, our approach allows the model to generate open-ended visual transformations to support subsequent reasoning. Across broad evaluation covering six visual reasoning tasks and multiple model backbones, REIMAGIN consistently improves over both text-only reasoning and strong specialist-tool baseline. This suggests that the benefit is not tied to single task, transformation, or model. Our results suggest two broader conclusions. First, image generation can act as general visual imagination mechanism within multimodal reasoning, reducing the need to engineer separate tool for each new transformation. Second, the effectiveness of this approach depends not only on the underlying models but also on the reasoning strategy used to decide what to visualize and how to use the result. The gains from automatic strategy discovery show that the models can leverage their understanding of visual transformations to discover relevant strategies without human-authored task-specific strategies or reasoning. An important next step is improving the reliability of generative visual reasoning. Our results suggest that this can come from stronger image generation models, better selection and verification of intermediate visualizations, and more scalable methods for discovering effective reasoning strategies. Overall, we view reasoning with image generation as promising step toward multimodal systems that can not only describe visual scenes, but also actively generate and transform them while solving complex problems. 10 Published as conference paper at COLM

sections.title: A Extended Related Work
sections.content: Visual reasoning with expert tools. To go beyond purely textual chain-of-thought, growing line of work equips Multimodal LLMs with visual tools that produce intermediate images the model can then reason over. For instance, Hu et al. (2024); Fu et al. (2025) introduce tool-augmented agents that call perception or editing operators such as crop, zoom, detection, segmentation, or depth estimation, composing them over multiple steps. Recent zoom-centric systems such as Pixel Reasoner (Wang et al., 2025b) and DeepEyes (Zheng et al., 2025) go further by training models to gather additional visual evidence through zoom-in or crop actions during reasoning, and similar tool-augmented frameworks have been developed for specialized domains (Wang et al., 2025a; Mallis et al., 2025; Sharrock et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2025). These systems remain bounded, however, by the tools available to them: each function performs narrow, pre-specified transformation, so the model can only carry out manipulations that have been implemented in advance. Open-ended transformations such as removing an arbitrary occluder, drawing hypothetical collision trajectory, or synthesizing counterfactual view are out of reach unless dedicated tool has already been built and the model is instructed to invoke it. In contrast, REIMAGIN replaces this fixed toolset with single instruction-following generative model that can perform wider range of visual transformations expressed in natural language, removing the need to engineer new tool for each new visual operation. Iterative refinement of generated images. separate line of work interleaves languagebased reasoning with repeated image synthesis, focusing on improving the final image itself rather than to solve downstream reasoning task. Yang et al. (2024) use GPT-4V to iteratively probe text-to-image model, propose revised prompts, and select among drafts. Guo et al. (2025) verify and reinforce image generation step by step using specialized reward models, Khan et al. (2025) have pretrained MLLM inspect each generated image against the users prompt and rewrite the prompt for the next synthesis round, and Wan et al. (2025) orchestrate multi-agent critique with tournament-based selection between iterations. In all of these settings, the focus is on the outputting an image that follows as much as possible the instructions of the user, whereas in our setting the image is an intermediate artifact and the goal is to answer downstream question. Reasoning with generative visual models. growing line of work explores using image generation to produce intermediate visual artifacts within reasoning process. Li et al. (2025) and Visual Planning (Xu et al., 2026) reason entirely through sequences of generated images, without textual chain-of-thought, and target individual narrow domains such as maze navigation and embodied planning respectively. DiffThinker (He et al., 2025) similarly reformulates reasoning as native image-to-image task using diffusion transformer, and is also evaluated on single domain of planning and spatial configuration problems. ThinkMorph (Gu et al., 2025) interleaves image generation with textual chain-of-thought, but the visual operations it considers, such as zooming and overlaying, overlap substantially with what fixed specialist tools can already provide, not demonstrating the diversity and flexibility that powerful image generators offer. Complementing these methods, Zeller et al. (2026) introduce benchmark that probes the limits of mental imagery in multimodal models. related line of work keeps the visual chain of thought internal, decoding continuous latent tokens rather than pixels. Each requires specialized training of the reasoning model, such as multi-stage distillation with reinforcement learning (Yang et al., 2026) or distillation from vision experts (Qin et al., 2025). Their scope is also limited: some are evaluated only on narrow domains like maze navigation and spatial planning (Zhang et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026), while others operate broadly but have not been shown to go beyond what specialists 15 Published as conference paper at COLM 2026 such as depth estimation or grounding already provide (Qin et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026). Finally, because their visual reasoning happens in latent space, the intermediate steps are not interpretable. In contrast, REIMAGIN is training-free and modular, and carries out its visual reasoning in pixel space, so every intermediate step is an explicit image that humans can directly inspect. Separately, recent work probes whether video generation models can serve as zero-shot visual reasoners by leveraging their learned world dynamics (Wiedemer et al., 2025); however, the generated video there is the final output being evaluated, rather than an intermediate artifact within broader reasoning loop. In contrast, we study training-free framework that interleaves text and image generation, evaluated across six diverse tasks with the same setup.

sections.content: Depth Perception. We use the validation split of BLINK (Fu et al., 2024), containing 124 instances, following the evaluation protocol of Visual Sketchpad (Hu et al., 2024). Collision Prediction. We randomly sample 100 instances from Spatial457 (Wang et al., 2025c). Multi-View Spatial Reasoning. We randomly sample 50 instances each from the Obj-Obj and Obj-Reg splits of MMSI-Bench (Yang et al., 2025), for total of 100 instances. Path Tracing. We programmatically generate 100 instances. To increase difficulty, the connecting lines are rendered as dashed rather than solid, and at least one pair of lines is designed to pass close to each other without intersecting.

sections.title: E Illustrative Example
sections.content: We illustrate one full reasoning trajectory on the SPATIAL457 collision-prediction task (Figure 4 top right). The input is an overhead scene image containing several coloured toy vehicles and the query What shape is the brown object that the large brown aeroplane hits if it moves forward? 1. Turn 1 Reasoning: The agent identifies the large brown aeroplane in the scene and notes that its forward trajectory is ambiguous because multiple objects lie in roughly the same direction. It decides that generated overlay showing single forward vector from the nose of the aeroplane would resolve the ambiguity. 2. Turn 1 Action: The agent calls generate_image( prompt="Draw one forward vector from the nose of the large brown aeroplane and circle the first object it hits. Lightly label brown objects only.", images=[scene_image] ) The tool returns an annotated image with forward arrow and circled target. 3. Turn 2 Context: The annotated image is appended to the context as new user message alongside the original scene. 4. Turn 2 Reasoning: Examining the overlay, the agent observes that the arrow terminates at rectangular brown object. It verifies the label against the original scene image to confirm the objects identity, then emits its final answer. 5. Turn 2 Termination: The agent outputs The first object hit is brown minivan. TERMINATE, and the answer Minivan is extracted. Without the intermediate visualization, no-tools baseline must reason about 3D trajectories purely from the original image, frequently confusing the aeroplanes heading with nearby objects and predicting the wrong collision target. The generated overlay reduces the problem to simple visual lookup, which the MLLM handles reliably. sections.content: We report the per-instance inference cost of REIMAGIN and the two baselines in Table 5, measured with Gemini-3.1-Pro as the MLLM and Nano-Banana-Pro as the visual generative tool, averaged over all task instances. REIMAGIN and Sketchpad are matched on every quantity that reflects reasoning effort: MLLM input tokens (19,700 vs. 21,000), output tokens (350 vs. 400), MLLM calls (1.79 vs. 1.83), and intermediate images produced (1.2 vs. 1.3), which yield an identical MLLM cost of $0.04 per instance for both methods. Both methods therefore spend essentially the same effort on reasoning, and neither obtains its accuracy by simply issuing more or longer MLLM calls. The two differ only in the cost and latency of image generation: Sketchpads intermediate images are produced by specialist vision models and incur no generationtoken cost, whereas REIMAGIN synthesizes them with frontier image model, adding 1,300 generation tokens and $0.12 per instance and raising median wall-clock time from 52 to 76 s. This is the price of replacing fixed set of specialist tools with single general-purpose generative one, and we expect it to fall as generative models become cheaper and faster. sections.title: I Ablating the Generative Tool
sections.content: The baselines in Table 1 differ from REIMAGIN in more than tool access: No Tools and Visual Sketchpad use their own prompts and their own agent scaffolds, so comparison against them cannot by itself attribute the observed gains to image generation specifically. To rule out these confounds, we ablate the generative tool within REIMAGIN itself while holding everything else fixed. Concretely, we replace generate_image with no-op that simply returns the input image it received, unchanged. The tool therefore remains available to the agent and is still invoked as usual, so the prompts, the tool definitions, the Python execution environment, and the programmatic image utilities are all identical to REIMAGIN; the only difference is that calling the tool no longer produces new visualization. This isolates the generative capability as the single variable that changes. As shown in Table 7, performance drops on all six tasks, with the largest decreases on path tracing (89.0 to 77.5) and puzzle completion (42.3 to 36.5). The ablated variant still outperforms the No Tools baseline in Table 1 on several tasks, which is expected given that it retains code execution and programmatic image manipulation, but it does not recover the full performance of REIMAGIN. Since the prompts and scaffold are identical across the two rows, the remaining difference is attributable to the generative tool alone, and not to prompt or scaffold differences between REIMAGIN and the baselines. The ablated variant replaces generate_image with no-op that returns the input image unchanged, keeping everything else identical: the same prompts, the same tool definitions, the same Python execution environment, and the same programmatic image utilities such as crop, overlay, and subtract_images. Because both rows share identical prompts and scaffolding, this comparison isolates the generative capability as the single variable, unlike the comparison against No Tools and Visual Sketchpad in Table 1, which also differ in their prompts and agent scaffolds. sections.title: J Faithfulness of the Generated Images
sections.content: REIMAGIN depends on the generative model producing an image that actually performs the transformation the agent requested. To measure how often this holds, we manually audited 120 generated images sampled across all six tasks, roughly 20 per task. Each image was labelled as faithful if it correctly carries out the requested transformation, for example if the occluder is genuinely removed, the trajectory line follows the stated heading, or the top-down map preserves the relative positions of objects, and unfaithful otherwise. We then paired each label with whether the agent ultimately answered the question correctly. For MMSI, where REIMAGIN applies test-time scaling, the audited image is the one chosen by the selector rather than an arbitrary sample, so the reported faithfulness reflects the images the MLLM actually reasons over. Of the audited generations, 75% are faithful. Conditioning on this label separates task outcomes sharply: the agent answers correctly in 87% of instances with faithful image, compared to 43% of instances with an unfaithful one. Unfaithful generations therefore account for substantial share of the remaining errors, consistent with the generation failures illustrated in Appendix K.1. This relationship is correlational, since instances that are harder for the generator may also be harder for the MLLM to reason about. The test-time scaling experiment in Figure 3 provides complementary evidence: sampling = 10 images and selecting the most faithful one improves spatial reasoning accuracy from 51.0% to 59.0% on Gemini-3.1-Pro and from 42.0% to 54.3% on Qwen-3.5-27B, while leaving the textual reasoning process untouched. Because the additional compute is spent only on sampling images, the resulting gain is attributable to improved faithfulness rather than to more reasoning. 24 Published as conference paper at COLM

sections.content: 41 Published as conference paper at COLM 2026 Figure 22: Qualitative examples of automatically discovered visual reasoning strategies. Discovered strategies are frequently similar to handcrafted ones, improving over text-only reasoning. 42 Published as conference paper at COLM 2026 Figure 23: Qualitative examples where REIMAGIN with the handcrafted strategy is more reliable than the discovered strategy. Top Left: In the Spatial task, the handcrafted strategy first creates unified view and then top-down blueprint of the scene. In contrast the discovered strategy simply creates panoramic image, which is not as helpful for the MLLM in some cases when trying to discern relative orientations, whereas the blueprint is. Top Right: When reasoning about collisions, the handcrafted strategy draws straight line through the object in question. The discovered strategy is similar, but in contrast draws single arrow, which forces the image generative model to decide what is the front or back of an object, or its direction. The image generative model might be worse at perception and reasoning, and hence this leads to worse performance in small number of cases. Bottom Left: In an occlusion question, the handrafted strategy of inpainting differs from the optimized one, which often draws grid or traces the missing objects over the occlusion. With less regular patterns, i.e. many chairs close to each other, such grid is not very helpful. Bottom Right: In the path tracing benchmark, the discovered strategy suggests to color the different lines instead of just making them solid. The image generative model sometimes struggles to maintain the consistency of color, which needs to be coherent across potentially quite distant parts of the image, in contrast to the local consistency of the solid line. Although the different colors make recognition easier for the MLLM, the image generative model sometimes makes these mistakes due to the more challenging request. 43 Published as conference paper at COLM

The upper left corner of the image is the origin (0, 0). All coordinates are normalized, i.e., the range is [0, 1]. All bounding boxes are in the format of [x, y, w, h], which is python list. is the horizontal coordinate of the upper-left corner of the box, is the vertical coordinate of that corner, is the box width, and is the box height. Notice that you, as an AI assistant, is not good at locating things and describe them with coordinate. You can use tools to generate bounding boxes. You are also not good at answering questions about small visual details in the image. You can use tools to zoom in on the image to see the details. Below are the tools in tools.py: ```python class AnnotatedImage: # class to represent an annotated image. It contains the annotated image and the original image. def __init__(self, annotated_image: Image.Image, original_image: Image.Image=None): self.annotated_image = annotated_image self.original_image = original_image def zoom_in_image_by_bbox(image, box, padding=0.05): """A simple wrapper function to crop the image based on the bounding box. When you want to answer question about visual details in bounding box, you would like to zoom in on the object using this function. Args: image (PIL.Image.Image): the input image box (List[float]): the bounding box in the format of [x, y, w, h]. padding (float, optional): The padding for the image crop, outside of the bounding box. Defaults to 0.1. The zoom factor cannot be too small. Minimum is 0.05 Returns: cropped_img (PIL.Image.Image): the cropped image Example: image = Image.open("sample_img.jpg") box = [x, y, w, h] # you can predict the bounding box coordinates yourself in the format [x, y, w, h] cropped_img = zoom_in_image_by_bbox(image, box, padding=0.05) display(cropped_img) """ def overlay_images(background_img, overlay_img, alpha=0.3, bounding_box=[0, 0, 1, 1]): """ Overlay an image onto another image with transparency. This is particularly useful visualizing heatmap while preserving some info from the original image. For example, you can overlay segmented image on heatmap to better understand the spatial relationship between objects. It will also help seeing the labels, circles on the original image that may not be visible on the heatmap. Args: background_img_pil (PIL.Image.Image): The background image in PIL format. overlay_img_pil (PIL.Image.Image): The image to overlay in PIL format. alpha (float): Transparency of the overlay image. bounding_box (List[float]): The bounding box of the overlay image. The format is [x, y, w, h]. The coordinates are normalized to the background image. Defaults to [0, 0, 1, 1]. Returns: PIL.Image.Image: The resulting image after overlay, in PIL format. Example: image = Image.open('original.jpg') depth_map = generate_image("create depth map of this image", image) overlayed_image = overlay_images(depth_map, image, alpha=0.3) display(overlayed_image) """ def generate_image(prompt: str, images: Image.Image = None, aspect_ratio: str = None): """ Generate an image using generative model. This is generalist tool that can generate images from text prompts or modify existing images based on prompts. It can be used to perform tasks like depth estimation, image segmentation, image generation, image editing, etc. Args: prompt (str): The text prompt describing the image to generate or the modification to make. images (PIL.Image.Image or List[PIL.Image.Image], optional): An optional single image or list of images to use as base or reference for generation. aspect_ratio (str, optional): The aspect ratio for the generated image (e.g., "16:9", "1:1", "4:3"). If provided, it will be used regardless of whether images are provided. If not provided and images are provided, the API will automatically match the first input image's aspect ratio. If not provided and no images are provided, defaults to "16:9". Returns: generated_image (PIL.Image.Image): The generated image Example: # Generate an image from text prompt generated_img = generate_image("A futuristic city skyline at sunset with flying cars") 44 Published as conference paper at COLM 2026 display(generated_img) # Generate an image based on an existing image and prompt input_img = Image.open("sample_img.jpg") modified_img = generate_image("Make this image look like watercolor painting", images=input_img) display(modified_img) Note: keep in mind that you can only feed single string as the prompt """ def pad_image(image: Image.Image, aspect_ratio: str): """ Pad an image with white background and center it to achieve specific aspect ratio. The original image is preserved at its original size and centered on white canvas. Args: image (PIL.Image.Image): The input image to pad. aspect_ratio (str): The target aspect ratio as string (e.g., "16:9", "1:1", "4:3"). Returns: padded_image (PIL.Image.Image): The padded image with the specified aspect ratio. Example: image = Image.open("sample_img.jpg") # Pad image to 16:9 aspect ratio padded_img = pad_image(image, "16:9") display(padded_img) # Pad image to square (1:1) aspect ratio square_img = pad_image(image, "1:1") display(square_img) """ def first_last_frame_to_video( first_frame: Image.Image, last_frame: Image.Image ): """ Generate video frames by interpolating between first frame and last frame using video generation model. This tool takes two images (first and last frames) and generates intermediate frames to create smooth video transition. The generated frames can be used for video analysis, motion understanding, or temporal reasoning tasks. Args: first_frame (PIL.Image.Image): The first frame of the video (start image). last_frame (PIL.Image.Image): The last frame of the video (end image). Returns: frames (List[PIL.Image.Image]): list of PIL Image objects representing the video frames in sequence. Example: first_frame = Image.open("start.jpg") last_frame = Image.open("end.jpg") frames = first_last_frame_to_video(first_frame, last_frame) for i, frame in enumerate(frames): print(f"Frame {i}: {frame.size}") display(frame) """ def subtract_images(image1: Image.Image, image2: Image.Image): """ Subtract image2 from image1, treating white pixels as zero. White pixels (value 255) are treated as zero in the subtraction operation. This means white areas contribute nothing to the subtraction, and darker areas contribute more. The result shows the difference between the two images, with white areas preserved from image1. Args: image1 (PIL.Image.Image): The first image (minuend). image2 (PIL.Image.Image): The second image (subtrahend) to subtract from image1. Returns: result_image (PIL.Image.Image): The result of image1 - image2, treating white as zero. Example: image1 = Image.open("image1.jpg") image2 = Image.open("image2.jpg") result = subtract_images(image1, image2) display(result) """ def generate_video(image, prompt: str, num_return_frames: int = 8): """ Generate video from an image and return sampled frames. This tool uses video generation model to generate video based on the input image and text prompt.
